title: Amul and the Dairy Cooperative
text:
In the 1940s dairy farmers in the Kaira district of Gujarat, India, had to sell their milk to a private dairy that held a contract to supply Bombay and paid them whatever it chose. Many owned only one or two buffaloes and had no bargaining power. Encouraged by the nationalist leader Vallabhbhai Patel, a local farmer and freedom fighter, Tribhuvandas Patel, organized them. In 1946 the farmers refused to supply the private dairy and formed their own cooperative union at Anand, starting with just two village societies.

In 1949 a young engineer named Verghese Kurien was posted to a government creamery in Anand. He did not want to be there and planned to leave, but Tribhuvandas persuaded him to stay and help the cooperative. Kurien stayed for the rest of his career. With his colleague H. M. Dalaya, he developed a way to make milk powder from buffalo milk, which experts had said could not be done, letting the cooperative process its surplus.

The structure was simple: farmers belonged to village societies, which owned the district union, which owned the processing plant. Farmers were paid fairly and regularly, according to the quantity and fat content of their milk. The brand name Amul was adopted in the 1950s.

The model spread to other districts. From 1970, under Operation Flood, led by Kurien's National Dairy Development Board, it was copied across India, which went on to become the world's largest milk producer.
lesson: Small producers who join together on fair rules can compete with powerful companies. Ownership by the members keeps the team's interests aligned.
people: Verghese Kurien, Tribhuvandas Patel, Vallabhbhai Patel, H. M. Dalaya
source: Verghese Kurien, I Too Had a Dream (2005)
